messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

James is a 37-year-old database administrator who nearly died from COVID-19 pneumonia two years ago. The illness struck without warning—what he thought was a mild cough escalated over three days until he was gasping for air in an emergency room, surrounded by masked staff, IV lines, and the rhythmic hiss of a ventilator. He remembers the sensation of drowning while fully conscious, the burning in his chest as doctors inserted a central line, the way his vision narrowed to a tunnel of fluorescent light before they sedated him. He spent eleven days intubated, and when he woke, his throat was raw, his arms bruised from blood draws, and his body felt like a foreign object that had betrayed him.

In the months after discharge, James tried to return to his routine, but his body refused to cooperate. At work—a sprawling data center with recycled air and a constant hum of servers—he found himself hyperaware of his own breathing. Every slight tightness in his chest sent a spike of alarm through him, and he would pause mid-keystroke to check whether his lungs still worked. The feeling never lasted, but the dread did. He stopped taking the stairs because the exertion left him breathless, and that sensation—that familiar, terrifying lack of air—was enough to trigger a cascade of physical reactions: his heart would hammer, his palms would sweat, and he would be back in that ICU bed, fighting for his next breath.

Avoidance became a quiet, daily discipline. He began restricting his eating, meticulously controlling portion sizes and meal times, because hunger and fullness felt like unpredictable bodily states he could no longer trust. He refused all invitations to exercise—jogging or weightlifting made his chest heave, and he was convinced that pushing his heart rate would bring back the collapse. More troublingly, he started dodging anything related to medicine. He ignored his annual physical, cancelled a routine colonoscopy, and took a longer route to work to avoid driving past the hospital where he had been treated. When a colleague mentioned donating blood, James felt his stomach turn and excused himself to the bathroom to sit on the floor until the dizziness passed.

The consequences accumulated quietly. His marriage, already strained by his irritability and hypervigilance, dissolved last year. His ex-wife told him he was "impossible to live with"—that he flinched whenever she touched his arm, that he snapped at her for coughing, that he spent every evening scanning his body for signs of danger. He couldn't argue. At work, his manager noticed he had declined three mandatory ergonomic evaluations and had taken unscheduled sick days whenever a flu shot clinic was held in the building. James knew he was risking his job, but the thought of a needle, of a medical professional’s gloved hands, of being examined like a specimen, was enough to make his throat close up.

What finally brought him to therapy was a simple, unavoidable trigger. His employer sent a company-wide email requiring everyone to complete a physical exam at an occupational health clinic by the end of the month, or face disciplinary review. James stared at the screen for twenty minutes, his chest tightening, his mind replaying the sensation of the endotracheal tube being removed. He realized he could not do it—could not sit in a paper gown, could not let someone palpate his abdomen, could not hear a stethoscope pressed to his ribs without falling apart. That evening, he sat in his empty apartment and told himself he was done running. He was terrified of the exam, but he was more terrified of the life he had built around avoiding it. He called a psychologist the next morning, hoping—though he would not say it out loud—that someone could help him learn to breathe again without flinching.
